subject: Medicine
summary: Acute abdomen is a sudden, severe abdominal pain requiring prompt evaluation. Clinicians must rapidly identify life‑threatening causes, differentiate surgical from medical conditions, and initiate appropriate treatment.

sections.p: Acute abdomen refers to sudden onset abdominal pain lasting less than 72 hours that may indicate a surgical emergency. Diagnosis combines history, physical exam, and targeted investigations.

t.b: Assess for infection or anemia; high WBC suggests infection, low Hb may indicate bleeding.
Elevated lactate (>2 mmol/L) indicates tissue hypoxia; causes include mesenteric ischemia, sepsis, or massive hemorrhage.

sections.p: Severity is graded by the presence of peritonitis, shock, or organ failure. The Ranson criteria for pancreatitis or the Mannheim Peritonitis Index for peritonitis help predict outcomes.

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, the top causes are appendicitis, perforated peptic ulcer, typhoid perforation, and intestinal obstruction. Tropical infections such as malaria, schistosomiasis, and HIV‑associated enteropathy also contribute.

sections.p: Patients often report sudden, worsening pain, nausea, vomiting, and inability to pass stool or flatus. Physical findings may include guarding, rebound tenderness, or absent bowel sounds.

t.b: Hypotension and tachycardia indicate shock; fever suggests infection.

faq.q: What is the most common cause of acute abdomen in children?
faq.a: Acute appendicitis is the most frequent cause in pediatric patients.

faq.q: Can malaria cause an acute abdomen?
faq.a: Yes, splenic rupture or severe intestinal involvement can present as acute abdomen.
Perforation, obstruction, or ischemia mandates emergency surgery.
